displayQuote: To err is human, to forgive, divine

meta.title: Who really said "To err is human, to forgive, divine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Alexander Pope wrote it in An Essay on Criticism (London, May 1711). The first edition reads "To err is Humane" — the 18th-century spelling of human.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To err is human, to forgive, divine'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified against Pope's 1711 first edition, where it closes Part II. But the first half was already an old proverb before Pope ever picked up a pen.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The couplet closes an argument about critics near the end of Part II of Pope’s An Essay on Criticism, first published in London in May 1711 — and it is legible in the first-edition facsimile. One caveat on wording: Pope’s printer set it as “To err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine,” because “humane” was then the ordinary spelling of “human.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
To what base Ends, and by what abject Ways,
Are Mortals urg’d by Sacred Lust of Praise?
Ah ne’er so dire a Thirst of Glory boast,
Nor in the Critick let the Man be lost!
Good-Nature and Good-Sense must ever join;
To err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine.
trail: May 1711 — Pope publishes An Essay on Criticism in London; the couplet sits near the end of Part II, at line 525 ↗. Wikisource dates first publication to 15 May 1711 ↗.
The first sheets — page 38 of the first edition prints “Good-Nature and Good-Sense must ever join; / To err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine,” as transcribed from the facsimile ↗.
1713 — the second edition carries the same wording; the Eighteenth-Century Poetry Archive ↗ sets its text from that printing and numbers the line 526.
1717 — Pope’s collected Works softens the punctuation and the capitals to “To err is humane, to forgive, divine” ↗ — one step from the version quoted today.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from page 38 of the 1711 first-edition facsimile on Wikisource, italics and capitals as printed. Line numbering varies slightly between printings: Wikipedia places the couplet at line 525, while the Eighteenth-Century Poetry Archive’s text of the 1713 second edition numbers it 526.

source.rightsNote: An Essay on Criticism was first published in London in 1711, so both the poem and its early printings are in the public domain in the United States. Wikimedia Commons carries the first-edition scan under an explicit public-domain mark, noting that it was published before 1 January 1931 ↗. No translation is involved — Pope wrote in English.

author.name: Alexander Pope
author.heading: About Alexander Pope
author.bio: Pope was born in London on 21 May 1688 and died at Twickenham on 30 May 1744, aged 56. As a Catholic under the Test Acts he was barred from university, from voting and from public office, and from the age of twelve Pott disease — tuberculosis of the spine — deformed his back and stopped his growth at four feet six inches; he made a living instead as the first English poet to get rich on subscription, largely through his verse translations of the Iliad and Odyssey. Wikipedia notes that he is often quoted in the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, with verses such as “damning with faint praise” and “to err is human; to forgive, divine” having entered common parlance.

misattribution.heading: What people still get wrong
misattribution.intro: Pope really did write it — this one survives the check. But two things about the line as it is quoted today are not his, and a third home it often gets given is simply wrong.

items.who: Not coined by Pope — an older proverb
items.why: “To err is human” was already a commonplace. Idiom Origins notes ↗ that Pope did not coin those words, and that the Latin errare humanum est had been current for centuries, often attributed to Plutarch. The closest classical wording with a real citation behind it is Cicero’s, in Philippica XII, 5 ↗: “Cuiusvis hominis est errare, nullius nisi insipientis in errore perseverare.” What Pope added — and what made it immortal — is the second half.

The couplet sounds like scripture and gets quoted as if it were, but it is not in the Bible. Idiom Origins states plainly ↗ that the saying did not originate in the New Testament, despite its Christian sentiment.

Every modern quotation silently updates Pope. The 1711 first edition ↗ reads “To err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine” — which, as Phrases.org.uk explains ↗, was not an error but the accepted spelling of the day.

misattribution.truthLine: The couplet is genuinely Pope’s, published in An Essay on Criticism in London in May 1711 ↗ — you can read it on the page of the first edition ↗.

context.heading: It was advice to reviewers, not a sermon
lead: Pope aimed An Essay on Criticism at critics, and the famous couplet is the punchline of a complaint about reviewers who make their names by savaging other writers. The lines just before it read “Ah ne’er so dire a Thirst of Glory boast, / Nor in the Critick let the Man be lost!” — so the forgiveness Pope calls divine is, in context, the standard he is setting for somebody holding a pen, as Interesting Literature reads it ↗.

The poem is didactic verse in heroic couplets — rhyming pairs of iambic pentameter — which is why a line meant as a rule for book reviewers detaches so cleanly and travels so far. Pope was a poet in his early twenties when it appeared in London in May 1711, and the couplet has been quoted loose from its argument ever since.
detailsBody: The 1711 sheets set the line as “To err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine.” That is not a typo and not a different word: Phrases.org.uk explains ↗ that “humane” was simply the accepted spelling of “human” in the early eighteenth century.

Pope’s own collected Works of 1717 already prints it in the softer form “To err is humane, to forgive, divine,” with a comma where the first edition had a semicolon — so the drift toward the modern reading began in the poet’s own lifetime, in a volume he supervised.
context.pull: Nor in the Critick let the Man be lost!
